Journal of Crystal Growth

Volume 292, Issue 2, 1 July 2006, Pages 505-509

Improved growth technology of large MgO single crystals

Author links open overlay panelXuZhangaDongfengXueaJiyangWangbXiqiFengc
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcrysgro.2006.04.058Get rights and content

Abstract

An improved growth technology (the arc-fusion method) has been successfully employed to grow large magnesium oxide (MgO) single crystals with an average size of 4–6 cm. Three adjustable graphite electrodes with different electric currents (IA>IB>IC) are applied, which technology is different from the conventional technology (using a uniform current). In addition, a proper control for the efficient use of different currents reduces the number of bubbles in the growth system, which allows us to obtain optically transparent high-purity MgO single crystals. Our present work shows that control of the temperature-gradient field in the whole process is the key to growing high-purity and large MgO single crystals.

1. Introduction

Crystal growth by the arc-zone melting technique has been used over the past decades to prepare single crystals of refractory metals and their alloys [1]. One particular benefit of the arc-zone melting technique is able to contain a volatile component in the preparation of alloys [2]. Such a technique can easily generate temperature up to 3600 °C in a short time. Since it is a cold hearth technique, arc melting avoids many problems with crucible contamination. On the basis of the arc-zone melting technique, an improved growth technology (i.e., an arc-fusion method) is currently applied to grow large magnesium oxide (MgO) single crystals.

MgO is a homomorphous compound (with a rocksalt structure) with ionic constituents of a relatively small number of electrons, which have a stable oxidation state. In recent years, MgO has become one of the preferred targets of surface structural analysis and catalytic research [3], and is an exceptionally important material for use in catalysis [4], toxic waste remediation [5], or as an additive in refractory, paint, and superconductor products [6], [7], [8]; it is also used in steel manufacturing because it is highly corrosion resistant [9]. Therefore, the growth of MgO crystals that are large enough to cut for further fabrications has become an interesting topic attracting the attention of materials scientists.

In the present work, the growth of large MgO single crystals using an arc-fusion method is reported. The optical characteristics of the obtained crystals are investigated by optical absorption spectra and X-ray excited luminescence (XEL) spectra, both of which indicate that the obtained samples are optically transparent high-quality MgO single crystals. In addition, to the best of our knowledge, no report is available showing the effect of temperature-gradient field on the growth of MgO single crystals. We present results concerning the effect of the spatial inhomogeneous temperature-gradient field on the growth of such single crystals. The growth process is discussed in detail, and shows that the crystal growth is a result of solid boundary migration.

2. Experimental procedure

The arc-fusion method developed on the basis of the arc-zone melting technique is most appropriate for the growth of large MgO crystals [10]. The diameter of the crucible can be up to 2000 mm and the height is 1700 mm. The crucible is made of stainless steel and can endure high temperature. The thermal field with proper temperature gradient in the crucible is established by designing the structure of graphite heating elements and controlling the input power on each element. The temperature-gradient field can be slightly adjusted by changing the vertical position of electrodes. Six temperature-measured points of thermocouples on average are distributed in the same layer, and these 12 layers (72 points) are far from the crucible bottom at from 300 to 1400 mm at intervals of 100 mm; they are used to record the temperature change in different parts of the crucible.

The optical absorption spectra were recorded on a Perkin-Elmer Lambda 9 UV-VIS-NIR spectrophotometer on the as-grown sample. The emission spectra were taken by exciting the sample with LD 940 nm as a pumping laser (excited at 940 nm). The light from the light source was chopped at 80 Hz and focused on the face of the sample. The emission from the sample was focused onto a monochromator and detected by a Ge detector. The signal was intensified with a lock-in amplifier and processed by a computer. XEL spectra were measured using an X-ray excited luminescence spectrometer, FluorMain, where an F-30 movable X-ray tube (W anticathode target) was used as the X-ray source, and operated under the same conditions (80 kV, 4 mA).

3. Results and discussion

A small starting electric current was used to generate the arc. To control the whole experimental process, the electric currents can be controlled by three electrodes. A minimum power input to the arc is required to grow MgO single crystals and this is related to the minimum temperature necessary to begin melting of the materials. The temperature field located in the growth system is not uniform; this nonuniformity can be explained by the design of different electric currents of the three electrodes. Three temperature-gradient fields are automatically formed in the growth system, which include the temperature field of the electrodes (FA, FB and FC), the temperature field between two electrodes (FAB, FBC and FCA) and the temperature field among the three electrodes (FABC), respectively. Additionally, FABC gradually rises with the continuous consumption of the three electrodes during the experimental process, and this forms the fourth temperature-gradient field in the growth system along the vertical direction. In this field the temperature at the top is higher than that at the bottom. It should be noted that the span of temperature variation is important for the resultant MgO single crystals. The sample is subjected not only to the temperature gradient determined by the temperature jump but also to the temperature gradient due to the crucible design. It should be emphasized that the latter gradient remains unchanged with time and is constant for specified sizes of the sample.

A distribution diagram of the temperature-gradient field in the growth system is shown in Fig. 1, from which we can find that the temperature of all measured points is equivalent at the beginning (T=0°C). Since the heating rate of the electrodes is the fastest, the temperature of the electrode range is obviously the highest at the end. Fig. 2 shows the time dependence of the temperature in the electrode range, from which we can find that the temperature of FA is the highest one among the three electrodes and that of FC is the lowest. The origin of this difference is the use of different currents (IA>IB>IC). Additionally, we also find that Figs. 2(a)–(c) can be divided into two parts. The first part is from 0 to 11 h, which is the heating stage with very steep slopes, in which raw materials melt and crystals gradually grow. The second is from 11 to 27 h, which is the heat preservation stage with a nearly constant temperature, in which crystals are purified. It can be found that the temperature continuously increases with the prolongation of reaction time from 0 to 27 h in Figs. 3(a)–(c), which differ from Fig. 2. In Fig. 3, the temperature between the A and B range is higher than that of the other two, which is also observed in Fig. 1.

The formed temperature-gradient fields in the whole process are the key to growing large MgO single crystals by this improved technique. The MgO crystals first nucleate in the melt having the lowest temperature, these nuclei are then used as the seed crystals, and MgO single crystals gradually grow as the nuclei boundaries migrate from the low temperature range to the high one. Finally, large MgO single crystals can be harvested. The preferential direction of the obtained large crystals is the 〈1 0 0〉 direction, which has been validated by our previous work [10]. The conventional method only forms one temperature field due to the use of the uniform current. When the reactive temperature is reduced, a large number of single nuclei are obtained simultaneously in the melt, which stunts the growth of large single crystals. However, the modified method forms four temperature fields in the growth system compared with the conventional one, thus avoiding the nucleation of a large number of crystals and creating favorable conditions for the growth of large MgO single crystals. Therefore, we believe that the new method is a better one for growing MgO single crystals of a large size. A photograph of the obtained crystal is shown in Fig. 4.

The gas included in the MgO crystals is collected at the top of the growth system in the heat preservation stage, which decreases the bubble number and increases the bubble volume in these crystals. The lower optical opacity of the obtained crystals is almost certain due to the fewer number and larger size of the bubbles in them. Both of these defects decrease the amount of light scattered from the crystals and make them more transparent than does the traditional method. Since it apparently results in an increased bubble size and not in an increased number per unit volume, even the greater fractional bubble volume observed in the obtained crystals aids in decreasing their opacity further. A UV transmittance curve of the obtained sample has also been reported in Ref. [10]. Average transmittance of the large MgO single crystal is more than 60% from 400 to 750 nm. Fig. 5 presents optical absorption spectra of large MgO single crystals obtained by the arc-fusion method in UV–VIS–NIR wavelength at room temperature. MgO possesses a steep absorption edge in the UV region (about 280 nm), which means that the strong photoabsorption of these crystals occurs only at wavelengths shorter than 280 nm. Fig. 6 shows XEL spectra of these crystals in which a very large emission band centered at about 740 nm can be observed.

4. Conclusions

MgO single crystals large in size and high in quality have been grown using the arc-fusion method. MgO crystals first nucleate in the low-temperature melting range, and then grow with the nuclei boundaries as they migrate from the low to the high temperature range. The effect of three temperature-gradient fields on the growth of MgO single crystals is discussed in detail: crystal quality can be improved by decreasing the bubble and defect numbers. Compared with the conventional method, the modified method is more appropriate for the growth of large MgO single crystal. We believe that this improved growth technology may also be applicable to grow other crystals at very high temperature, opening a new path to crystal growth technology.
